title: India Will Lift AFSPA From Nearly All of the Northeast by Next Year. Amit Shah Says the Region Has Earned It.
excerpt: The Home Minister's announcement at the NITI Aayog meeting signals that India's most controversial security law is heading for its narrowest-ever footprint in the region — and that the Northeast is being reimagined as an economic frontier.
body:
Amit Shah has been signalling for years that the Armed Forces Special Powers Act is on its way out in the Northeast. On Thursday, at the margins of the NITI Aayog Governing Council meeting in New Delhi, he put a timeline on it.

"We will remove AFSPA from entire Northeast barring one or two states by next year," the Home Minister said, according to Press Trust of India.

The statement is the most definitive commitment any Indian government has made to winding down one of the country's most controversial security laws in the region where it has been in force, in various configurations, since 1958. AFSPA gives the armed forces sweeping powers in designated 'disturbed areas,' including the authority to search, arrest and use force — protections that human rights groups have challenged for decades and that local populations have bitterly opposed.

## What Has Changed

The Northeast's security landscape has transformed over the past decade. Major insurgent groups in Assam, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya and Mizoram have either signed peace accords or entered ceasefire agreements. The Bodo Accord of 2020, the Karbi Anglong Agreement of 2021, and multiple framework agreements with Naga groups have collectively reduced armed violence to levels not seen since the 1960s in several states.

AFSPA has already been progressively withdrawn. It was lifted from Tripura in 2015 and Meghalaya in 2018. In 2022, the government reduced its footprint in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Shah's announcement suggests that by next year, the law could remain in force in only one or two states — most likely parts of Nagaland and Manipur, where the final status of the Naga peace talks and the ethnic tensions that erupted in Manipur in 2023 remain unresolved.

## The Economic Calculation

The AFSPA rollback is not just a security decision. It is an economic one. The Northeast sits at the crossroads of India's Act East Policy, the gateway to ASEAN markets through Myanmar and Bangladesh. But private investment has been sparse, in part because the 'disturbed area' designation has functioned as a de facto investment warning.

Removing AFSPA changes the risk calculus for investors. It signals stability. It also removes a legal framework under which land acquisition, business operations and civil rights operate under different rules than the rest of the country.

The timing aligns with several infrastructure projects nearing completion in the region. The Bogibeel Bridge connecting Assam's north and south banks, the Barak Valley-Manipur rail line, and upgrades to airports in Imphal, Dimapur and Shillong are creating physical connectivity that the region has lacked. Without AFSPA's shadow, these projects can function as genuine economic arteries rather than strategic military corridors.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

The Northeast has a significant but often overlooked diaspora. Communities from Assam, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram are present across the US, UK, Canada and Australia — many of them having left during periods of active conflict. For this diaspora, AFSPA has been more than a law. It has been a symbol of why they left and a barrier to returning.

The rollback opens possibilities that were previously theoretical. Tourism infrastructure — the Northeast has some of India's most spectacular landscapes, from Meghalaya's living root bridges to Nagaland's Hornbill Festival — can now attract serious private capital. Small and medium enterprises, particularly in food processing, handicrafts, bamboo products and organic agriculture, can operate without the regulatory uncertainty that AFSPA's provisions created.

NRI entrepreneurs from the Northeast have long talked about investing back home. Shah's timeline gives them something they have not had before: a date by which the security framework will look fundamentally different.

## The Caveats

Shah said 'one or two states' would retain AFSPA. The identity of those states matters enormously. If Manipur is one of them — and the ethnic divide between Meitei and Kuki communities remains unresolved — then the rollback will be incomplete in the state that has most visibly suffered under the law.

Nagaland's status depends on the progress of the Naga peace talks, which have been in various stages of negotiation for over two decades. A final accord would remove the last justification for AFSPA in the state. Without one, the law's continuation becomes a political choice rather than a security necessity.

The announcement also raises implementation questions. AFSPA's removal requires a formal notification by the government that a previously 'disturbed area' is no longer disturbed. The armed forces have historically resisted such notifications, arguing that premature withdrawal risks undoing hard-won security gains.

But Shah's statement, made at a meeting attended by every chief minister in the country, carries the weight of a public commitment. Walking it back would carry political costs that the current government appears unwilling to pay.

nri_angle: AFSPA's rollback opens the Northeast to the kind of private investment and tourism that has been impossible under military-administered zones — creating opportunities for NRI entrepreneurs and diaspora community projects in one of India's most culturally rich but economically isolated regions.
